nameStory: The Clover Weevil gets its name from its favorite dining spot – clover patches! Like many weevils, it's named after its host plant where both adults and larvae do their feeding. The 'weevil' part comes from the Old English 'wifel,' meaning beetle, perfectly describing these small, hard-shelled garden visitors.
description: The Clover Weevil is a small, brownish beetle about the size of a grain of rice, typically measuring 3-5mm long. Like all weevils, it has a distinctive elongated snout (called a rostrum) that looks like a tiny elephant trunk. Its body is oval-shaped and covered in fine, bristly hairs that give it a slightly fuzzy appearance. This introduced species from Europe has become a common sight in New England's lawns, gardens, and wild spaces where clover grows.

idTips.label: Elongated Snout
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic long, curved snout extending from the head – it's unmistakably weevil-like and feels hard when gently touched

idTips.label: Bristly Body
idTips.description: The entire body is covered in fine, stiff hairs that give it a slightly rough, fuzzy texture when handled gently

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: About rice-grain sized with an oval, somewhat flattened body that fits easily on your fingernail

idTips.label: Brown Coloration
idTips.description: Typically grayish-brown to dark brown, sometimes with subtle mottled patterns that help it blend with soil and plant debris

idTips.label: Clover Association
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near clover plants, where they create small, round notches along leaf edges

idTips.label: Movement Pattern
idTips.description: Moves slowly and deliberately, often dropping to the ground and playing dead when disturbed

habitat: Clover Weevils thrive anywhere clover grows in New England – from suburban lawns and park spaces to agricultural fields and roadside verges. They prefer areas with white clover, red clover, and other legumes, often found in slightly disturbed soils with good drainage. Look for them in sunny to partially shaded locations from sea level to moderate elevations throughout the region.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active on warm days, beginning to feed on young clover leaves. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving around during the day.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible feeding and mating. Look for characteristic crescent-shaped notches they chew along clover leaf edges.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding to build up energy reserves for winter. Late fall is when they begin seeking shelter under leaf litter and debris.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter hidden under leaves, mulch, or other ground cover. They're dormant and rarely visible unless you disturb their hiding spots on warm winter days.

funFact: Clover Weevils are actually helping your lawn stay green! Their larvae live in root nodules and don't harm the clover, but the adult's feeding triggers the plant to produce more nitrogen-rich growth, which benefits surrounding grass – making them accidental lawn care assistants.
confusionNotes: Other small brown weevils can look similar, but the Clover Weevil's strong association with clover plants is your best clue. If it's not on or very near clover, it's probably a different weevil species. Remember: 'Clover Weevil, clover leaves' – they rarely stray far from their favorite food.
contextualKnowledge: As an introduced species from Europe, Clover Weevils arrived in North America accidentally through agricultural trade. While they're considered a minor pest of clover crops, they're generally harmless in home landscapes and have become part of New England's naturalized fauna.
compareHints: Since this is the only Sitona species commonly found in New England, compare it with other small weevils in the True Weevil family. Clover Weevils are distinguished by their bristly body texture and strong clover association, while most other small weevils in the region are either smoother-bodied or found on different host plants like dandelions or grasses.
